newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish inflation seen at the foot of curve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish inflation seen at the foot of curve.

text.p: Sweden reported on Tuesday a falling annual inflation trend for the third month running but, analysts said, consumer prices are set to rise.
Swedish consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in December, against market expectations for a 0.3 percent drop, which gave a year-on-year fall of 0.2 percent. Average inflation for 1996 was 0.7 percent.
"It's still low interest rate costs that are pulling the figure," economist Tomas Niemela from broker Aragon said.
"The figures are still good, and we are now seeing the bottom."
Unibank Markets analyst Bjorn Englund said the figure was in line with expectations and would rise next month.

"The after-Christmas sales have affected prices somewhat. We have now seen the bottom of CPI. From, and starting in January, we will see an increase with a year-on-year rise in January of 0.2 to 0.3 percent," Englund said.
Sweden's central statistics bureau (SCB) said the monthly CPI fall was due partly to lower mortgage rates and partly to slight price cuts on clothes, shoes and telecoms services.
Analysts said higher energy prices also hit the CPI.

"It is a little higher than expected. It probably is because of higher energy prices, but...there is probably no inflationary pressure on core prices yet," said J P Morgan economist Katharina Hoyland.
Most analysts had expected the central bank, the Riksbank, to cut its key interest rate, the repo, by 15-25 basis points at its weekly tender, held 15 minutes after the CPI data.

But the rate, the bank's key tool for controlling money market liquidity, was left untouched at 4.10 percent. This prompted debt yields to rise, signalling there had been expectations of a cut in the market.

However some analysts expected the Riksbank board to cut the repo at a meeting on Thursday. The repo rate stands in centre of the bank's interest rate corridor between the deposit and lending rates of 3.75 and 5.25 percent respectively.
The meeting follows a spate of economic data due out this week including November retail sales and industrial production on Wednesday and Sweden's trade balance early on Thursday.
However, others said it meant the Riksbank was taking a wait-and-see view on rate cutting and would probably take a break before trimming the repo again.
Last year the Riksbank cut the rate 25 times from a level of 8.91 percent in January 1996.
James Stewart, economist at S-E-Banken, told Reuters the Riksbank was taking a more cautious stance and would probably wait to see the January inflation data before making a move.
"There's a great deal of debate in the market about exactly where the (inflation) rate will be in January. We think it's going to be around zero percent or so," he said.
"Assuming the favourable trend in the inflation is confirmed from January onwards the Riksbank could commence cutting the rate."
Economist James McKay of Paine Webber also said it was unlikely the Riksbank would cut the rate on Thursday, but said he saw a 50 basis point cut in the repo rate over coming weeks.
"Key rate cuts are on the cards as well. I do expect a 50 basis point repo cut and that would suggest the deposit rate would have to be cut," McKay told Reuters.
